--- title: "Types of learning" description: "Some data come with answers and some do not. Supervised learning predicts a known answer; unsupervised learning looks for groups. One method of each, k-nearest neighbours and k-means, on the coastal survey the whole course uses." order: 1 categories: [foundations, supervised, unsupervised] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## The data decide the kind of learning Machine learning comes with a long list of names: regression, classification, clustering, random forests, neural networks. They are easier to hold on to once you can place them on a map. The first division on that map depends on the data you hold rather than the method you choose. **Supervised learning** learns from examples with a known answer. Each example has some measurements, the **inputs** (also called features), and the answer, the **outcome**. The model learns to get from the inputs to the outcome, so that it can predict the outcome for a new example from its inputs alone. A known outcome is also called a **label**, especially when a person assigned it, as when a specialist names the species in an image. The outcome sets the task: **regression** when it is a quantity, such as a number of animals, and **classification** when it is a category, such as "present" or "absent". **Unsupervised learning** has no outcome at all. It receives a table of measurements and looks for structure in it: groups of similar examples, or variables that move together. Nothing tells it which answer is right, so its results need extra care. A third kind, **reinforcement learning**, learns from the consequences of its own actions: an autonomous underwater vehicle might learn a sampling route by trial, rewarded for each useful measurement. It needs a way to act and a reward, not a table of data, and this course does not cover it. ::: {.diagram} ![Three kinds of learning. Supervised learning has an answer for every example; unsupervised learning has none and looks for groups; reinforcement learning acts, receives a reward, and adjusts. The table shows the first five stations of the survey.](img/learning-types.svg){fig-alt="Three panels. The supervised panel shows a table of five stations with columns for temperature, salinity and depth, and a highlighted answer column, found, reading yes, no, no, yes, yes. The unsupervised panel shows grey points by temperature and depth, falling into three dashed circles. The reinforcement panel shows a box for an underwater vehicle above a box for the sea, joined in a loop: an arrow labelled action, move and sample, runs down to the sea, and an arrow labelled reward and new position runs back up."} ::: ## One coastal survey runs through the course ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: Every example in this course uses the same dataset: a simulated survey of stations on a temperate coastal shelf. At each station the survey measured the water and counted one species of seabed animal. This page uses five of its columns: - **temperature**, the water temperature, in °C; - **salinity**, in practical salinity units (PSU), close to grams of salt per kilogram of seawater; - **depth**, in metres; - **abundance**, the number of animals counted at the station; - **present**, "yes" if at least one animal was found, "no" otherwise. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() survey |> select(station_id, temperature_c, salinity_psu, depth_m, abundance, present) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station_id | temperature_c| salinity_psu| depth_m| abundance|present | |:----------|-------------:|------------:|-------:|---------:|:-------| |ST0001 | 11.15| 33.26| 99.2| 15|yes | |ST0002 | 4.42| 34.20| 134.7| 0|no | |ST0003 | 14.69| 33.67| 52.3| 0|no | |ST0004 | 10.02| 33.47| 90.8| 21|yes | |ST0005 | 6.35| 34.22| 125.0| 1|yes |
::: ::: The survey has 800 stations and more columns than these five; [The coastal survey](../02-marine-data/the-coastal-survey.qmd) introduces them all. ## k-nearest neighbours predicts from the most similar stations Every model on this page is asked about the same three new stations. They are made up for illustration and are not part of the survey. We call them shallow, mid-depth and deep, from their depths; the models see only the three measurements. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new_stations <- tibble( station = c("shallow", "mid-depth", "deep"), temperature_c = c(12, 9, 5), salinity_psu = c(33.4, 33.7, 34.2), depth_m = c(40, 90, 150) ) ``` ::: The simplest supervised method is **k-nearest neighbours**. To predict for a new station, it 1. measures how far the new station is from every survey station, across temperature, salinity and depth at once; 2. picks the *k* nearest survey stations, here 15; 3. predicts from their answers: for presence, the share of them where the species was found; for abundance, their average count. There is no equation to fit. The survey itself is the model, and predicting means looking up the stations most like the new one. "How far" needs care, because the three inputs are measured in different units. Depth spans about 190 metres and salinity about 2.2 units, so without adjustment depth alone would decide which stations are nearest. **Scaling** puts the inputs on a common scale: subtract each input's mean and divide by its standard deviation, so that every input is measured in standard deviations. ### Presence is a classification With presence as the outcome, the task is a classification. In tidymodels, a **recipe** lists the outcome and the inputs and prepares the data, here by scaling. A workflow joins the recipe to the model, so the new stations are scaled in the same way as the survey before the model sees them. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Every neighbour counts equally. knn <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 15, weight_func = "rectangular") |> set_engine("kknn") presence_recipe <- recipe(present ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = survey) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) classifier <- workflow() |> add_recipe(presence_recipe) |> add_model(set_mode(knn, "classification")) |> fit(survey) bind_cols(select(new_stations, station), predict(classifier, new_stations, type = "prob")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred_yes| .pred_no| |:---------|---------:|--------:| |shallow | 0.67| 0.33| |mid-depth | 0.73| 0.27| |deep | 0.47| 0.53|
::: ::: For each new station the model returns the share of its 15 nearest survey stations where the species was found, and the share where it was not. That share is its estimate of the chance of finding the species: 67% at the shallow station, 73% at the mid-depth one and 47% at the deep one. ### Abundance is a regression Change the outcome to the number of animals counted and the same survey becomes a regression problem. The method stays the same; only the last step changes, from a share to an average. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} abundance_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = survey) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) regressor <- workflow() |> add_recipe(abundance_recipe) |> add_model(set_mode(knn, "regression")) |> fit(survey) bind_cols(select(new_stations, station), predict(regressor, new_stations)) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred| |:---------|-----:| |shallow | 3.07| |mid-depth | 3.53| |deep | 1.40|
::: ::: The model expects about 3.1 animals at the shallow station, 3.5 at the mid-depth one and 1.4 at the deep one. It gives a prediction for any station but no number that says how much depth or temperature matters. [Prediction and explanation](prediction-and-explanation.qmd) asks when that matters. ## k-means sorts the stations into groups without an answer Now remove the answers entirely: no abundance, no presence, only temperature, salinity and depth. We ask **k-means clustering** to sort the 800 stations into three groups, called **clusters**. Despite the shared letter, its *k* is the number of groups, not a number of neighbours. It works in four steps: 1. Place three group centres among the stations, at random. 2. Assign every station to its nearest centre. 3. Move each centre to the average of the stations assigned to it. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until no station changes group. "Nearest" is measured on scaled inputs, for the same reason as before. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = survey) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) clusters <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(k_means(num_clusters = 3) |> set_engine("stats")) |> fit(survey) clustered <- bind_cols(survey, extract_cluster_assignment(clusters)) clustered |> summarise( stations = n(), `depth (m)` = round(mean(depth_m)), `temp (°C)` = round(mean(temperature_c), 1), `salinity (PSU)` = round(mean(salinity_psu), 2), .by = .cluster ) |> arrange(`depth (m)`) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.cluster | stations| depth (m)| temp (°C)| salinity (PSU)| |:---------|--------:|---------:|---------:|--------------:| |Cluster_1 | 241| 45| 10.5| 33.36| |Cluster_3 | 296| 89| 9.2| 33.74| |Cluster_2 | 263| 133| 6.3| 34.07|
::: ::: The three groups follow depth: shallow and warm, mid-depth, and deep and cold. That is no surprise, because in this survey the three variables move together: salinity rises with depth, and temperature falls with it. The cluster numbers themselves mean nothing; k-means numbers its groups in whatever order it happens to find them. ## k-means groups differ in a species they never saw Ask both kinds of model about the three new stations. The supervised classifier gives a chance of presence; k-means gives a group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_cols( select(new_stations, station), predict(classifier, new_stations, type = "prob") |> select(.pred_yes), predict(clusters, new_stations) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred_yes|.pred_cluster | |:---------|---------:|:-------------| |shallow | 0.67|Cluster_1 | |mid-depth | 0.73|Cluster_3 | |deep | 0.47|Cluster_2 |
::: ::: The classifier's answer is about the species, because the species was its target. k-means returns only a number, `Cluster_1` to `Cluster_3`, which says nothing on its own. To give the groups names, the code below sorts them by the average depth of their stations, shown in the table above, and calls them Shallow, Mid-depth and Deep. The names are ours; k-means knows only the numbers. With names attached, the groups can be compared with something k-means never saw: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Name each cluster after the average depth of its stations. depth_order <- clustered |> summarise(depth = mean(depth_m), .by = .cluster) |> arrange(depth) |> mutate(group = c("Shallow", "Mid-depth", "Deep")) clustered <- clustered |> left_join(select(depth_order, .cluster, group), by = ".cluster") |> mutate(group = factor(group, levels = depth_order$group)) group_summary <- clustered |> summarise(stations = n(), `species present` = round(mean(present == "yes"), 2), `mean abundance` = round(mean(abundance), 2), .by = group) |> arrange(group) group_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|group | stations| species present| mean abundance| |:---------|--------:|---------------:|--------------:| |Shallow | 241| 0.81| 4.94| |Mid-depth | 296| 0.82| 4.26| |Deep | 263| 0.69| 2.52|
::: ::: The species turns up at 81% of shallow stations, 82% of mid-depth ones and 69% of deep ones, and the average count falls from 4.94 in the shallow group to 2.52 in the deep one (@fig-clusters). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_space <- ggplot(clustered, aes(depth_m, temperature_c, colour = group)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", colour = NULL, title = "The groups k-means found") p_abund <- ggplot(clustered, aes(group, abundance, fill = group)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) + guides(fill = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Abundance", title = "Abundance in each group", subtitle = "k-means did not use abundance") p_space + p_abund + plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: stations by depth and temperature, coloured by the group k-means assigned. Right: abundance in each group. The clustering never saw abundance, yet the groups differ in it.](types-of-learning_files/figure-html/fig-clusters-1.png){#fig-clusters fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a scatter plot of temperature against depth, with points coloured into three groups that mostly follow depth, with some overlap: shallow and warm on the left, mid-depth in the middle, deep and cold on the right. The right panel is a boxplot of abundance for each group; the shallow group has the highest median and the deep group the lowest.' width=1700} ::: ::: | | Supervised | Unsupervised | | --- | --- | --- | | Needs | An answer for every survey station | Only the measurements | | Returns | A prediction of the answer | A group, with no meaning attached | | Can be checked | Against stations held back, whose answers are known | Only indirectly, against things it never saw | | Example here | The chance of presence | Shallow, mid-depth and deep groups | So the groups do differ in the species, although k-means never saw a single catch. This is unsupervised learning at its most useful and its most tempting. Ask for six groups and you get six, each just as confidently defined. [Checking a pattern before reporting it](../08-unsupervised-learning/interpreting-patterns.qmd) covers the checks that tell a real structure from an artefact of the method. ## Labels can be wrong, and groups depend on the set-up **Unsupervised does not mean assumption-free.** Choosing k-means, choosing three groups, choosing the variables and their scaling: each is a modelling decision, and each shapes the groups. **Labels are often less solid than they look.** Two specialists classifying the same seabed images disagree more often than most people expect. A supervised model can never be more reliable than the labels it learned from. **The boundaries blur in practice.** Some methods combine a few labels with many unlabelled examples, or build labels from the data's own structure. The division on this page is a teaching map, not a law. [Discriminative and generative models](discriminative-and-generative-models.qmd) adds a second division, by the thing the model learns. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Supervised learning needs examples with known answers. Regression predicts a quantity, classification a category. - k-nearest neighbours predicts a new case from the most similar cases in the data, and the same method does classification and regression. - Unsupervised learning has no answers. Methods such as k-means find groups, and will always return as many as you ask for. - Methods that measure how near two cases are need their inputs scaled first. - A supervised model is no more reliable than its labels; an unsupervised one is shaped by the choices made in setting it up. ::: ## Try it yourself Refit the classifier with `neighbors = 1`, then with `neighbors = 200`. Which of the three new stations changes most, and why does a single neighbour give only 0% or 100%? Refit the clustering with `num_clusters = 6`, then with `num_clusters = 2`. Do the groups still look like real habitats? Which evidence would make you prefer one answer over another?
